job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Rafael Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I keep a schedule, otherwise the days blur. Mornings are applications, I send about twelve a week and log each one in a spreadsheet with the date and any reply. After lunch I study for the first paper of my professional accounting exams, two hours, and then I help my dad Lars with his plumbing invoices in the evening. I live in Kellerton with my parents and my two younger brothers.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Accounting, with a good result. I spent eight weeks at a small tax practice, preparing returns for self-employed people and small firms, mostly sole traders like my dad. I do use AI now and then, for looking up tax rules or checking my own work, but I wait until other people have used a tool for a while before I trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say sensible, the sort of thing I expected. At the practice I'd tell the partners the tools are fine for the dull parts, and the judgment still belongs to the accountant. With friends I'd say don't panic, but keep learning anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means my plan doesn't change. I pass the exams, I land a job at a mid-size firm, and I do the work I trained for. The small catch is that routine return preparation gets a little cheaper, so there might be a bit less of the entry-level work I did on the internship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: twelve applications a week, the exam papers on schedule, and a monthly coffee with Mr Dube, the partner from my internship, who said he'd keep me in mind. I'd also use AI a little more for checking my own work. And I'd keep helping my dad with his books, because it keeps me sharp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly even. I'm a bit impatient about the job, otherwise fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you wait for others to try a tool first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why do you wait for others to try a tool first?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good first year at a firm look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen it get things wrong with tax numbers. I'd rather be second and right, because in my field a mistake costs someone real money. By the time I use something, I want a colleague to have already found the traps.

say: I'd say it's **sensible**: the tools help with dull parts, but judgment still belongs to the accountant.
I'd tell friends not to panic and keep learning.

Keep helping my dad with his plumbing books.
feel: **Even**: a bit impatient about the job, otherwise fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change how firms work, and the sensible response is to adapt in steps. At the practice I'd say we should try the tools on small jobs first and check each result. With friends I'd say there's no point shouting at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the first rung of accounting is the part that shrinks. Return preparation, reconciliations and checking are tasks I did on the internship, and software handles them quickly. A firm might hire three graduates instead of eight, and I need to be in the three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen my search to include advisory, payroll and small business accounting, where clients still want a person. I'd take a short course in data analysis and spend a few weeks properly learning the AI tools my future boss will expect. I'd also ask Mr Dube if there's any contract work. And I'd keep my savings steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense, but workable. I can see a way through if I keep making small moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the three out of eight be chosen from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Where would the three out of eight be chosen from?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the search would you widen first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ones who can show they've worked with the tools and can explain a result to a client. So I'd write down what I've done: a spreadsheet model, a reconciliation checked by software, a note on where it went wrong. That's the evidence a partner wants.

I'd tell friends there's no point shouting at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too short for anyone to prepare, and I'd say it plainly at the firm. I'd ask for transition plans, a bit of public money for retraining and some limit on how fast firms can swap staff. Not a ban, just a pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the graduate route is the first to close. If a machine does any thinking job cheaper, a firm doesn't need an eight-week intern or a new graduate. My professional exams would be worth far less than I hoped, and my cushion would not last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pull my money into a savings account and stop spending on anything extra. I'd apply to jobs where the client wants a person, like small business advice or the tax office, and I'd consider my dad's trade for a while. I'd ask Lars to teach me how plumbing quotes work, since that business has to stay with people for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a lot of lists. I'd feel like I was spreading my chances across five baskets without knowing which one holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your two younger brothers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell your two brothers?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would the cushion really last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brothers Mats and Jonas, who are 16 and 14, to learn a skill that needs hands. I'd say learn finance as a second thing. I'd say not to bet everything on one door. It's the opposite of what I did, and I'd feel a bit guilty.

say: I'd say **two years** is too short to prepare and ask for transition plans and retraining money.
I'd ask for a pace limit, not a ban.
think: The graduate route is the first to close, and my exams would be worth **far less** than hoped.
My cushion would not last forever.

steps.text: Move spare money into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is real time, enough to plan if you start now. At the practice I'd propose a training programme for new graduates working with the tools. I'd tell friends to pick one skill to go deep on rather than a little of everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm in a decent place if I move this year. A job in the next twelve months gives me years of experience before the end point. If I'm still looking in two years, I'd be competing with graduates who use the tools better than I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a firm job by spring and finish the exam papers in the evenings. I'd learn the firm's software properly and offer to run the small AI pilots, since nobody else wants to. I'd save about 30 percent of my pay and look at buying a small flat with my girlfriend Ines by 27. And I'd keep investing a little in an index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. A bit of weight, but I can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you volunteer for the AI pilots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why would you volunteer for the pilots?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would buying a flat with Ines depend on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's where the learning is, and a partner remembers the graduate who raised a hand. If the firm is going to change anyway, I'd rather be the person helping decide how.

I'd tell friends to go deep on one skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous and the main risk is people doing nothing with it. I'd press the firm and the government to plan for the people who retire, retrain or change careers. I'd tell friends to use the time to build skills that aren't just numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel safe if I behaved well. I'd pass the exams, work three or four years at a firm, then move into something advisory or run my own small practice. The part I'd watch is the last four years, when the software gets really good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job as soon as possible, keep studying and save up. Around 25 I'd move out with Ines, and by 30 I'd have either a senior role or a small practice with Mr Dube. I'd put a bit of money in each month, and I'd stay in touch with my brothers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Ten years gives me room to be sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a small practice offer that a big firm can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would a small practice offer that a big firm can't?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch in those last four years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clients who want a name and a face. A client who trusts me gets advice no software can give, because I know their busy seasons and their family. That's the bit I'd build on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, because there's no time to turn a plan into a track record. What would help is firms that still take on beginners, retraining money that arrives quickly, and being allowed to try the tools at work without being blamed for mistakes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I plan a lot because I'm nervous, not because I'm confident. The spreadsheet is how I stay calm, and I know a spreadsheet can't tell me what's coming.

headlineQuote: I plan a lot because I'm nervous, not because I'm confident.
portrait: Rafael is 23, an accounting graduate in Kellerton, living with family, with a full **application spreadsheet** and no offer.
He studies for professional exams and does part-time books for his plumber father.
His centre views make him seek a **pace** for change, not a ban.
He uses AI occasionally and waits for others to find the traps first, which suits tax numbers.
His planning hides nerves; he wants firms to keep hiring beginners and **tolerate mistakes**.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries him most, because there is no time to turn a plan into a track record.
whatWouldHelp: Firms that still take on **beginners** and fast retraining money.
Room to try tools at work without being blamed for mistakes.
